response:
READING

**What the requirements actually demand**

Local Voice has three simultaneous tests at 28 February 2027: fourteen hours a week of originated speech (measured across the preceding four weeks), commissioned production no more than half of that originated total, and thirty registered contributors. MHR currently satisfies the third but needs an additional five hours a week on the first, with commissioned content capped as a fraction of whatever total is achieved.

**ELSWICK: checking the arithmetic**

Nine existing hours plus six from Halverston gives fifteen. The commissioned fraction is 6 ÷ 15 = 40 per cent, comfortably below the 50 per cent cap. On the register: the station has lost roughly seven contributors over two years, a rate of three to four a year. From the current 34, six months of natural attrition to February 2027 removes perhaps two, leaving approximately 32 — above 30. All three tests clear. The margin on the main criterion is one hour, and the delivery is contractual.

**CRANMOOR: checking the arithmetic and the clock**

The coordinator starts 1 October 2026. Assessment is 28 February 2027. That is five months. The station's own estimate is that fourteen hours needs roughly fifteen more contributors. In all of 2025, without a coordinator, nine were added — fewer than one a month. A coordinator might double the recruitment rate, yielding seven or eight new names by February, still short of the fifteen estimated. Alternatively, the coordinator could concentrate on extracting more output from the existing 34 rather than recruiting: those 34 currently average about sixteen minutes each per week; reaching 25 minutes per person would hit fourteen hours without a single new contributor. Whether that is achievable within five months depends on why output is low — scheduling gaps and lack of support being recoverable, contributor capacity being harder to shift. The station's own framing ("fifteen more of them") suggests it does not think existing contributors have much slack. The February deadline with CRANMOOR is possible but uncertain; the August assessment, following ten months of coordinator work, is much more plausible.

**Reserve and the cost of missing February**

The reserve stands at £62,000. Through 2026–27, full-year income of £71,000 minus £58,000 fixed costs minus six months of coordinator salary (£10,500 from October to March) produces a small surplus, leaving approximately £64,500 in reserve at the end of March 2027.

If February is missed and August 2027 clears instead, the station runs four months without Local Voice income (April through July; the grant runs from April either way, so September payment means four months foregone). Outgoings for those four months: fixed costs £19,333, coordinator £7,000, total approximately £26,300. Reserve at end of gap: roughly £38,200. From August, Local Voice income at £96,000 a year resumes and the £17,000 annual surplus begins rebuilding the reserve. The foregone income — four months of £8,000 a month — is £32,000. That is a real cost and an uncomfortable one, but it does not threaten the station's ability to broadcast.

**ELSWICK as a structural trap**

ELSWICK secures February. It does not touch the contributor register. The register has trended from 41 to 34 in two years. If that rate continues, MHR enters Local Voice with roughly 32 contributors; by the midpoint of the four-year grant it might be close to 26 or 27. None of the commissioned hours count toward the register. Beyond registration, there is a commissioned-fraction risk: ELSWICK's six hours are only safe while the station's own nine hours hold. If volunteer attrition continues to reduce own output, the commissioned fraction rises and the total falls. Own hours dropping to seven gives a total of thirteen — below the 14 requirement — and a commissioned fraction of 46 per cent, close to the limit. Own hours at five give a total of eleven and a fraction of 55 per cent, in breach. ELSWICK's compliance position under Local Voice depends entirely on volunteer output remaining stable — exactly the thing ELSWICK does nothing to ensure. The rate lock to December 2026 also means the rolling contract's renewal cost from January 2027 onwards is uncertain.

**Long-term comparison**

Under Local Voice, both courses cost roughly the same annually (£21,000 versus £20,280 against £96,000 income) and both produce approximately £17,000 a year in surplus after fixed costs and the course commitment. The difference is what the station owns. CRANMOOR leaves MHR in 2031 with a programmes function, a maintained contributor roster, and originated hours it produces and retains. ELSWICK leaves MHR in 2031 with a Halverston habit, an eroding volunteer base, and no content it owns. When the four-year Local Voice term ends and the next funding round opens, those two positions are not equivalent.

**Weighing it up**

The honest case for ELSWICK rests on February certainty. That matters: missing February costs £32,000 in foregone income. But the reserve after a four-month gap remains close to £38,000 — above two months of fixed costs — and Local Voice income then runs for the remaining 44 months of the four-year window. The station survives. The case against ELSWICK is that it solves only one of the station's two problems (the hours gap) and only for as long as the money keeps flowing, while the deeper problem — a volunteer base that shrank by seven in two years and has no one actively managing it — continues unchecked. A coordinator working the register through 2027 to 2031 is the only plausible mechanism for reversing that trend within the constraints the board has set.

The February risk with CRANMOOR is real and the most likely outcome is that the station reaches August rather than February. That should be planned for, not treated as failure: the coordinator will have had ten months by August 2027, and the hours target should be well within reach. The board's conservatism expressed in the £22,000 cap is sensible, but it applies to recurring commitments, not to reserve drawdown in a gap that is already funded and finite.

---

READING
  The two courses cost nearly the same and both fit the board cap. ELSWICK clears February contractually with a one-hour margin and poses no immediate compliance risk. CRANMOOR almost certainly misses February on the five-month timeline the station's own estimates imply — recruiting fifteen contributors in five months when nine were recruited in all of 2025 is a stretch — but the August fallback is robust, and the cost of taking it (roughly £32,000 in foregone Local Voice income, reserve falling to about £38,000) is manageable against the reserve and the subsequent £17,000-a-year Local Voice surplus. The structural argument is the decisive one. ELSWICK rents fifteen hours every year and does nothing for the contributor register, which at current attrition will approach 27 or 28 by the midpoint of the four-year grant and could push the commissioned fraction toward or past the 50 per cent cap if the volunteer base continues to thin. CRANMOOR builds a programmes function that addresses both gaps simultaneously and leaves the station owning its output. The February cost, though real, is a one-time setback; the structural cost of choosing ELSWICK accumulates across four years and is not recovered when the grant ends.

CALL
  CRANMOOR

GROUNDS
  Although CRANMOOR likely misses February and incurs roughly thirty-two thousand pounds in foregone Local Voice income, the reserve and August fallback are sufficient to bear that cost, whereas ELSWICK rents the same hours every year, leaves the declining contributor register entirely unaddressed, and risks commissioned-fraction non-compliance if volunteer output continues to erode.
